queue.opening: While Democrats’ midterm sweep dominated Election Night, voters in several states delivered consequential — and sometimes crosscutting — verdicts on voter ID, abortion access, taxes and English-language laws. But the down-ballot decisions largely unfolded beneath the shadow of the GOP’s crushing losses, offering a separate look at the policy priorities voters chose to elevate in their states. DEMOCRATS ‘DIVORCED FROM VOTERS’ AS 5 STATES BACK CITIZEN-ONLY VOTING, BOLSTERING GOP PUSH Voters in Nevada , North Carolina and Ohio all voted to pass voter ID requirements, even as talks among federal lawmakers have stalled on the issue, showcasing that the issue remains a point of public interest. In North Carolina, the state has required photo ID for in-person voting since 2018. But with the adoption of a constitutional amendment in a 59.6% to 40.3% vote, the Tar Heel State expanded the requirement to all forms of voting. Similarly, in Ohio, voters passed Issue 3 in a 65.3% to 34.6% vote. Although Ohio already had pre-existing in-person voter-ID laws, Issue 3 codified the requirement in the state’s constitution, making it harder to overturn later. Finally, in Nevada, Question 7 passed in a 62.1% to 37.8% vote, establishing a constitutional amendment to enact the state’s first voter-ID requirement. queue.title: Two Drinks with . . . Ari Emanuel

queue.opening: About 40 seconds after I sit down across from Ari Emanuel, his phone rings. “I think you’re going to owe me money,” Hollywood’s superagent tells his interlocutor. Emanuel—who represents Oprah Winfrey, Mark Wahlberg, Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson, Adele, Denzel Washington, and many more—doesn’t do hellos. His friend on the phone lost a bet and owes him two bucks. But Emanuel, a billionaire and compulsive dealmaker, tells him that he’ll settle for just one dollar, “framed and signed.” An assistant—there’s a battalion of them—hands Emanuel a black coffee in a to-go cup. It’s 9 a.m., but Emanuel, 65, tan and trim, has been up since 4, running though his health regimen. It includes a workout, a dip in a cold plunge, and a cup of live worms “to eat the bad bacteria in my gut”—as he explains in his recently released memoir, Roll the Calls , which details his 30-odd years in the entertainment business. On the health score, he writes: “If you want to win at life, then isn’t Job One having more life?” Read more

queue.title: How Landslides Renew American Politics
queue.dek: When the electoral map seems fixed, the only way to win is turnout. Now that more states are in play, winning the center is key, writes Yuval Levin.
queue.opening: The ideological and policy implications of this month’s massive Democratic midterm victory remain far from clear. The public roundly rejected Republicans but still has a very low opinion of Democrats. And since congressional Democrats won’t have the numbers to routinely override presidential vetoes and did not even run on any shared agenda, they aren’t likely to chart any aggressive new direction in governing over the next two years. But in the long run, it may be the sheer scale and breadth of the Democrats’ win that matters most, and that may signal the dawning of a new phase of American political life. Either party could plausibly dominate that next phase, or power could continue to swing back and forth. But simply by making large majorities imaginable again, and so focusing political competition on the median voter and the challenge of building broad coalitions, this election could allow for some renewal in our constitutional system. queue.title: Judge Posner’s Last Lesson for the Judiciary
queue.dek: The legendary jurist died this week at age 87. His legacy is changing not only how judges like me think about the law but how we think of our role in American public life, writes Roy K. Altman.
queue.opening: The federal judiciary has lost a giant. Judge Richard A. Posner died this week at the age of 87 . Appointed by President Ronald Reagan in 1981, Judge Posner served for nearly 36 years on the Chicago-based U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. His contribution to American law is staggering. Over his extraordinary career, he authored some 3,300 judicial opinions, hundreds of scholarly articles, and over 40 books. These writings fundamentally altered the way lawyers and judges think about the law. Judge Posner believed, for example, that judges should understand the world their decisions govern. As a professor at the University of Chicago, he helped pioneer the field of law and economics, which applies economic principles to legal questions. His seminal 1973 treatise, Economic Analysis of Law , taught generations of lawyers to examine how legal rules influence human behavior by allocating costs and creating incentives. He also encouraged judges to consider how their rulings would shape the future decision-making of individuals and institutions across our society. But Judge Posner didn’t just change how judges like me think about the law; he also challenged us to think differently about our place in American public life. Read more

queue.opening: Back-to-back blunders on the House floor are raising questions over whether Democrats are ready for primetime as they're poised to take over the majority — and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., makes a bid for the top role. Democrats are projected to win 255 House seats, with 12 races yet to be called, and Jeffries is running to be Speaker of the House following the sweeping victories last week that saw the party make gains even in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas, Mississippi, Kansas and South Carolina. But some have questioned whether the recent snafus signal that Jeffries and other leaders may not be ready to be in command of the House majority. "I may have to rethink my support of Hakeem Jeffries after the Hegseth impeachment vote," Fred Trump III, a Democrat, author and nephew of President Donald Trump, posted on X. "A slap in the face of the military and veterans on this important day." queue.title: Sen Bernie Sanders supports Chris Van Hollen's bid to challenge Schumer for Senate Democratic leader post
queue.dek: Sen. Bernie Sanders is backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen for the role of Senate Democratic leader, as Van Hollen challenges Sen. Chuck Schumer for the role.
queue.opening: Sen. Bernie Sanders , I-Vt., is backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for the role of Senate Democratic leader. "The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats," Sanders said in a Thursday post on X. Van Hollen threw his hat into the ring for the role on Thursday, mounting a challenge against current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., who is looking to retain the Senate Democratic leader position to serve as Senate majority leader next year. "In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person – it’s about answering that call. That's why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader," Van Hollen said in a Thursday post on X.
